mainTopic: The versions of the question sent to רבי ירמיה, and how to read unclear or conflicting amounts in a שטר
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier question: why does the משנה say something as obvious as "one witness is not enough"? The גמרא answers that it is teaching that two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid by Torah law, just like one witness on a פשוט. Next, אמימר brings a proof that one written witness and one oral witness can join together, from a question the scholars of ארץ ישראל sent to רבי ירמיה. רב אשי, מר בר חייא and רבינא each tell that question differently: two courts, judges from two courts, or a court of three where one judge died. In every version רבי ירמיה humbly answers, and because of his answer he was brought back into the בית מדרש. A new משנה then teaches how to read a שטר whose amounts conflict or are partly erased. If the amounts disagree, the holder gets the smaller one. If the number is erased, he gets two coins. If the top and bottom disagree, the bottom amount decides. The גמרא then brings a ברייתא about vague words like 'silver' and 'gold' in a שטר. It explains, through רבי אלעזר and רב פפא, why these words mean at least one full דינר.

steps.title: The question on the משנה comes back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה is still hard to explain: why does it state something obvious?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is still a difficulty!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the earlier discussion by saying the problem with the משנה is still there. Why would the משנה tell us something that seems obvious?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that a document with only one witness signed on it is invalid, and that seems too obvious to need saying. After the earlier back-and-forth, the גמרא admits this question has not gone away. That sets up the answer in the next step.

phrases.english: The mishna is still a difficulty!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִיתִין!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion by saying the question on the משנה's wording still stands. Step 2 answers it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the משנה that rules a document with one witness is invalid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that ruling is obvious, the משנה should not need to state it.

steps.title: Two witnesses on a tied document are like one witness on an ordinary document
steps.stepSummary: The משנה puts the two cases side by side to teach that two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid by Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what the משנה teaches us: two witnesses on a tied document are like one witness on an ordinary document. Just as there the problem is by Torah law, so too here the problem is by Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ruling about one witness is in the משנה only to teach us about another case. Two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid at the same level as one witness on a פשוט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By itself, the one-witness ruling would be obvious. But the משנה lists it next to the case of two witnesses on a מקושר to show that both are equal. One witness on a פשוט is clearly invalid by Torah law, so two witnesses on a מקושר must also be invalid by Torah law (פסולא דאורייתא), and not only by rabbinic law.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us (the new point)

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה compares the two cases to teach that two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid by Torah law, just like one witness on a פשוט.
steps.whyThisMatters: It tells us the problem with a מקושר that lacks enough witnesses is a Torah-level problem, not just a rabbinic rule.

phrases.english: It teaches us this:
that two witnesses on a tied document
are like one witness on an ordinary document.
Just as there, the disqualification is by Torah law,
so too here, the disqualification is by Torah law.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 1 by explaining what the משנה is really teaching.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the obvious-looking ruling is there to teach about a different case by comparison
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid only by rabbinic law.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two witnesses on a מקושר are invalid by Torah law, just like one witness on a פשוט.

steps.title: The question sent to רבי ירמיה: can a written witness and an oral witness join together?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts bringing support for the earlier idea that one written witness and one oral witness combine. It quotes a question sent to רבי ירמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, because the scholars sent this question from ארץ ישראל to רבי ירמיה: if there is one witness in writing and one witness who speaks, can they join together?
steps.whatsHappening: This step sets up a proof. The גמרא quotes the question the scholars asked רבי ירמיה. Step 4 clarifies the question, and step 5 gives his answer, which completes the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תדע means a proof is coming for the earlier view that a witness signed on a document can join with a witness who testifies in person. The question is about one witness signed on a loan document and another who speaks about the same loan in court: do they count together as two witnesses? The way this question is handled will be used as the support.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (this is so): it introduces a proof
They sent from there (from ארץ ישראל)
That they join together (to count as two witnesses)

steps.confusionAlert: This step only asks the question. רבי ירמיה's answer comes in step 5, after the גמרא clarifies the question in step 4.

phrases.english: Know that this is so,
as the colleagues sent from there to Rabbi Yirmeya:
one witness in writing
and one witness orally,
what is the law: do they combine?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּדַּע, דִּשְׁלַחוּ מִתָּם חַבְרַיָּיא לְרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves away from the משנה's wording and starts a proof for the earlier view about combining a written witness with an oral witness.
steps.raayaObject: The view that one witness in writing and one witness speaking in person can combine
steps.raayaSupportSource: The question the scholars of ארץ ישראל sent to רבי ירמיה (answered in step 5)

steps.title: Pinning down exactly what was asked
steps.stepSummary: The question to רבי ירמיה cannot follow the תנא קמא, who does not even combine two written or two oral testimonies. So it must follow רבי יהושע בן קרחה: does his rule also cover one written witness plus one oral witness?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the first תנא who argues with רבי יהושע בן קרחה, don't ask, because even two in writing or two orally don't combine. Ask only according to רבי יהושע בן קרחה: is it only two written or two oral that combine, but not one written and one oral? Or is there no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is spelling out the exact question that was sent to רבי ירמיה. It shows which opinion the question must be based on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא is strict: even two written testimonies or two oral ones don't join. So under his view, one written plus one oral surely doesn't join, and there is nothing to ask. רבי יהושע בן קרחה does combine two-and-two, so the open question is whether he would also combine a mixed pair: one written and one oral.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed Sage in a ברייתא or משנה
You should not ask (the answer is obvious)
They combine (join into one valid testimony)
Or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'two in writing and two orally' as one big group of four witnesses. It means two written testimonies, or two oral testimonies, each combining with its own kind.

phrases.english: According to the first tanna
phrases.notes: This points back to a ברייתא where the first תנא and רבי יהושע בן קרחה argue about combining testimonies.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה – לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ,
phrases.english: who argues with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, you should not ask,
for even two in writing
or two orally do not combine.
Rather, when should you ask?
According to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנַיִם בִּכְתָב וּשְׁנַיִם עַל פֶּה הוּא דְּמִצְטָרְפִי,
phrases.english: is it only two in writing or two orally that combine,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל עֵד אֶחָד בִּכְתָב וְאֶחָד עַל פֶּה
phrases.english: but one witness in writing and one orally
we do not combine;
or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: אליבא דתנא קמא דרבי יהושע בן קרחה לא תיבעי לך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the content of the question to רבי ירמיה that Step 3 introduced.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Under רבי יהושע בן קרחה, does one written witness combine with one oral witness, or only two-and-two?

steps.title: רבי ירמיה answers: they combine
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה humbly replies that he leans toward saying the written and oral witnesses do combine. This supports the earlier view.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent to them: I am not worthy of what you sent me, but this is how your student's opinion leans: that they combine.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the question. He says one written witness and one oral witness do combine. This finishes the proof the גמרא began bringing in Step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was whether a mixed pair (written plus oral) combines under רבי יהושע בן קרחה. רבי ירמיה says yes. That directly supports the idea from Step 3 that one written and one oral witness join together.

phrases.english: He sent to them:
I am not worthy
that you should send to me;
but this is how the opinion of your student leans:
phrases.notes: 'Your student' is רבי ירמיה humbly talking about himself.

phrases.english: that they combine.

steps.triggerLanguage: שלח להו אני איני כדיי ששלחתם לי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the answer to the question defined in Step 4, completing the proof.
steps.raayaObject: That one witness in writing and one witness orally combine.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי ירמיה's reply to the colleagues: 'they combine.'

steps.title: רב אשי tells the story differently
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that in his tradition, the question sent to רבי ירמיה was not about written and oral witnesses. It was about two witnesses who testified in two different courts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We teach it this way. The colleagues sent to רבי ירמיה: Two witnesses testified, one in this court and one in that court. May one court come to the other court so the testimonies combine?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on the proof. He says the original question was about something else entirely: two witnesses in two separate courts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the question was about two courts and not about written plus oral, then רבי ירמיה's answer 'they combine' says nothing about written and oral witnesses. So the proof from Step 5 falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: The colleagues (the scholars of the academy)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a proof depends on knowing the exact case. Change the case, and the same answer proves something else.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי speaking to אמימר, who brought the proof from רבי ירמיה.

phrases.english: We teach it like this:
that the colleagues sent to Rabbi Yirmeya:
Two who testified,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד בְּבֵית דִּין זֶה, וְאֶחָד בְּבֵית דִּין זֶה;
phrases.english: one in this court and one in that court;

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ בֵּית דִּין אֵצֶל בֵּית דִּין,
phrases.english: what is the law: may one court come to the other court
and they combine?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה אנן הכי מתנינן לה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 5 by giving a different version of the question.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from רבי ירמיה's answer.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question was really about two separate courts, not about written plus oral witnesses.

steps.title: In רב אשי's version, the question follows רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: Under the תנא קמא, separate testimonies don't combine even in one court, so there is nothing to ask. The question only works under רבי נתן: does his combining work only in one court, or also across two courts?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the first תנא who argues with רבי נתן, don't ask, because even in one court they don't combine. Ask only according to רבי נתן: is it only in one court that they combine, but not in two courts? Or is there no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רב אשי's version of the question using the same pattern as Step 4, but now based on רבי נתן's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן allows combining testimonies that were not given together, but only clearly within one court. The open question is whether this also works across two courts. In this version, רבי ירמיה's 'they combine' is about two courts, not about written plus oral witnesses.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions of the question to רבי ירמיה. In the first version, it was about written plus oral witnesses, so it supports combining them. In רב אשי's version, it was about two courts under רבי נתן, so it proves nothing about written plus oral.

phrases.english: According to the first tanna who argues with Rabbi Natan,
you should not ask,
for even in one court
they also do not combine;
rather, when should you ask?
According to Rabbi Natan:
is it in one court that they combine,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בִּתְרֵי בֵּי דִינָא לָא מִצְטָרְפִי;
phrases.english: but in two courts they do not combine;
or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: אליבא דתנא קמא דרבי נתן לא תיבעי לך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out רב אשי's version of the question, the same way Step 4 spelled out the first version.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Under רבי נתן, do separate testimonies combine only within one court, or also across two courts?

steps.title: רבי ירמיה answers in רב אשי's version: the two courts combine
steps.stepSummary: In רב אשי's version, רבי ירמיה humbly replies that testimony given in two different courts does combine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he sent back to them: 'I am not worthy of the question you sent me. But this is how your student's opinion leans: they should combine.'
steps.whatsHappening: In רב אשי's version, רבי ירמיה answers the question about two witnesses who testified in two different courts. He says their testimonies combine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the same humble words we saw in step 5, but here they answer a different question. In רב אשי's version the answer only means that, according to רבי נתן, testimonies combine even across two courts. So this answer no longer supports combining one written witness with one oral witness.

keyTerms.meaning: your student (רבי ירמיה humbly calls himself their student)

steps.confusionAlert: The words are the same as in step 5, but they answer a different question. Only the question has changed.

phrases.english: And he sent to them:
I am not worthy
of what you sent to me,
but this is how the opinion of your student leans:
that they should combine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁלַח לְהוּ: אֲנִי – אֵינִי כְּדַיי שֶׁאַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question as framed in רב אשי's version in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to רבי נתן, do testimonies combine across two different courts?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רבי ירמיה leans toward saying they combine.

steps.title: מר בר חייא's version: combining one judge from each court
steps.stepSummary: מר בר חייא says the question was about two witnesses who testified in one court and again in another court. Can one judge from each court come and be combined?
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר חייא said: This is what they sent him: two witnesses testified in this court, and then testified again in that court. What is the law if one judge comes from each court, and they combine?
steps.whatsHappening: A third version of the question sent to רבי ירמיה is given. This time it is about combining judges, not witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the same two witnesses testified together in both courts, so the witnesses themselves are complete. The new question is whether one judge from each court can join together. Like רב אשי's version, this version also has nothing to do with written and oral testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: the אמורא who gives a third version of the question

phrases.english: מר בר חייא said:
This is what they sent to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is רבי ירמיה, the same person the question was sent to in the earlier versions.

phrases.english: two who testified in this court,
and then testified again in that court:

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶחָד מִכׇּל בֵּית דִּין
phrases.english: what is the law if one comes from each court,
phrases.notes: "One" here means one judge from each court.

phrases.english: and they combine?

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר בַּר חִיָּיא אָמַר, הָכִי שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third version of the question to רבי ירמיה, different from both the first version and רב אשי's version.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can one judge from each of two courts that heard the same witnesses be combined?

steps.title: The question only works according to the תנא קמא
steps.stepSummary: Under רבי נתן the answer is obvious: if witnesses combine, judges surely do. So the question must follow the תנא קמא: maybe only witnesses don't combine, but judges do?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי נתן you should not ask this. Now that we combine witnesses, do we even need to ask about judges? Rather, when should you ask it? According to the תנא קמא who argues with רבי נתן. Is it only witnesses that we don't combine, but judges we do combine? Or perhaps there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא works out which opinion this question must follow. It shows that the question only makes sense under the תנא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן combines separate witnesses, so combining judges would surely be fine according to him. The תנא קמא does not combine separate witnesses. Maybe judges are different and can still be combined, or maybe the rule is the same for both. This is the opposite of step 7, where the question only worked under רבי נתן.

keyTerms.meaning: now that X is true, do we even need to ask about Y?
the first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה
or perhaps there is no difference

steps.confusionAlert: In step 7 (רב אשי's version) the question only worked under רבי נתן. Here (מר בר חייא's version) it only works under the תנא קמא. Don't mix up the two versions.

phrases.aramaic: אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי נָתָן לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ –
phrases.english: According to רבי נתן, you should not ask this:
now that we combine witnesses,
do we even need to ask about judges?
Rather, when should you ask it?
According to the תנא קמא who argues with רבי נתן:
is it only witnesses that we do not combine,
but judges we do combine?
Or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי נָתָן לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains which opinion מר בר חייא's question follows, and what exactly is being asked.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to the תנא קמא, are judges different from witnesses, so that judges from two courts can be combined?

steps.title: רבי ירמיה answers in מר בר חייא's version: the judges combine
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה gives the same humble reply: his opinion leans toward saying they combine.
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back to them: 'I am not worthy of the question you sent me. But this is how your student's opinion leans: they should combine.'
steps.whatsHappening: In מר בר חייא's version, רבי ירמיה answers that the judges from the two courts do combine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words are the same as before, but here they mean that even the תנא קמא, who does not combine separate witnesses, would combine judges. So in all three versions so far רבי ירמיה gives the same answer, but each version has a different question. Only the first version supports combining written and oral witnesses.
steps.whatToRemember: So far there are three versions of the question to רבי ירמיה (רבינא gives a fourth in the next step): (1) one written witness plus one oral witness, under רבי יהושע בן קרחה; (2) רב אשי: two witnesses in two courts, under רבי נתן; (3) מר בר חייא: one judge from each of two courts, under the תנא קמא. In these three the answer is 'they combine'. Only version 1 supports the earlier idea.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because the question has different versions, the proof from רבי ירמיה's answer for combining written and oral witnesses is not certain.

phrases.english: He sent to them:
I am not worthy
of what you sent to me,
but this is how the opinion of your student leans:
that they should combine.
phrases.notes: Here "they" means the judges from the two courts.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לְהוּ: אֲנִי – אֵינִי כְּדַיי שֶׁאַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question as framed in מר בר חייא's version in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to the תנא קמא, can judges from two courts be combined?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רבי ירמיה leans toward saying they combine.

steps.title: רבינא's version: one of three judges died after ratifying a document
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the question sent to רבי ירמיה was about three judges who confirmed a שטר, after which one of them died. Must the remaining two write that they were three and one is gone?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: this is what they sent him. Three judges sat to confirm a document, and one of them died. Do the others need to write, 'We were sitting as a court of three, and one is no longer here,' or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more version of what the question to רבי ירמיה really was. This time it is about a court of three where one judge died before signing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A court that confirms a שטר needs three judges, but here only two can sign. The question is whether they must state on the document that a third judge was there, so nobody thinks only two judges ran the court.

keyTerms.meaning: Confirming a document in court by checking the witnesses' signatures
'We were sitting as a court of three'
He is not here (no longer present or alive)
An אמורא who gives his own version of the question

phrases.english: Ravina said: this is what they sent to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רבי ירמיה. This is one more version of the question from the earlier steps.

phrases.english: Three who sat to confirm the document,
and one of them died;
do they need to write
'We were sitting as a court of three,
and one is not here,' or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר, הָכִי שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a fourth version of what the question to רבי ירמיה was, alongside the first version and the versions of רב אשי and מר בר חייא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must two surviving judges write that the court had three members and one is no longer present?

steps.title: רבי ירמיה answers that they must write it
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה again humbly says he is not worthy of the question. He answers that they must write 'We were a court of three, and one is not here.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He sent back to them: I am not worthy of what you sent me. But your student's opinion leans this way: they must write, 'We were sitting as a court of three, and one is not here.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers this version with the same humble opening. He rules that the two judges must write that a third judge was there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without that line, the document would look as if only two judges confirmed it, which is not a valid court. Writing it shows the court really had three judges.

keyTerms.meaning: Your student (רבי ירמיה humbly calls himself this)

phrases.english: He sent to them: I am not worthy
of what you sent to me,
but this is how your student's opinion leans:
that they need to write:
'We were sitting as a court of three,
and one is not here.'

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לְהוּ: אֲנִי – אֵינִי כְּדַיי שֶׁאַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in רבינא's version.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, they must write that the court was three and one is no longer present.

steps.title: Because of this answer, רבי ירמיה was brought back into the study hall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the story: because of this answer, the חכמים let רבי ירמיה back into the בית מדרש.
steps.simpleTranslation: And because of this, they brought רבי ירמיה into the study hall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the whole story about the questions sent to רבי ירמיה. It tells us how it ended: he was allowed back into the בית מדרש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His answer was humble and correct, whichever version of the question we accept. That earned him his place back among the חכמים.
steps.whatToRemember: Every version of the question gets the same humble reply from רבי ירמיה, and in the end he is welcomed back into the בית מדרש.

phrases.english: And because of this, they brought in
Rabbi Yirmeya into the study hall.
phrases.notes: He had been sent out of the study hall earlier in this מסכת (דף כג עמוד ב).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל דָּא עַיְּילוּהוּ לְרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בְּבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story that began with the questions sent to רבי ירמיה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי ירמיה's humble, correct answers led the חכמים to bring him back into the בית מדרש.

steps.title: New משנה: a document whose two amounts don't match
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if a שטר states an amount in זוזים and also in סלעים, and the two don't match, the holder collects only the smaller amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a document says '100 זוזים, which are 20 סלעים,' he gets only 20 סלעים. If it says '100 זוזים, which are 30 סלעים,' he gets only a מנה (100 זוזים).
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic: a document that writes one amount in two different coins, and the two numbers don't agree. The משנה says the holder gets the lower amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סלע equals 4 זוזים, so 100 זוזים should be 25 סלעים. In the first case the סלע number (20 = 80 זוזים) is lower, so he gets that. In the second case the זוז number (100) is lower than 30 סלעים (120 זוזים), so he gets the 100. Either way, the person holding the document only collects the smaller figure.

keyTerms.meaning: A silver coin, also called a דינר

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the זוז number always wins or the סלע number always wins. The rule is to take whichever amount is smaller, and that is a different coin in each case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a basic rule for reading documents that contradict themselves: the one collecting gets the lower amount. The גמרא will next look into the reasoning behind it.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If it is written in it:
'One hundred zuz, which are twenty sela' –
phrases.notes: A סלע is 4 זוזים, so 100 זוזים is really 25 סלעים. The two numbers don't match.

phrases.english: he has only twenty.
phrases.notes: Twenty סלעים, which is 80 זוזים, the smaller amount.

phrases.english: 'One hundred zuz, which are thirty sela' –
he has only a maneh.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ כָּתוּב בּוֹ: זוּזִין מְאָה, דְּאִינּוּן סִלְעִין עֶשְׂרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a brand new topic. It has no link to the story about רבי ירמיה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a document's two amounts contradict each other, the holder collects only the lower amount.

steps.title: When the number after a plural coin word is erased, assume two
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if a שטר says 'silver זוזים', 'silver סלעים' or 'דרכונות', and the number was erased, the lender collects only two of that coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the שטר says 'silver זוזים that are...' and the rest was erased, it is no less than two. The same is true for 'silver סלעים that are...' and for 'דרכונות that are...'.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה keeps going with rules for reading a damaged שטר. Here, the coin word is still there but the number was erased.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The coin word is plural, so the debt must be at least two coins. Because the lender has to prove what he claims, he gets only the smallest amount the plural word can mean, which is two.

keyTerms.meaning: זוזים, silver coins (a זוז is the same as a דינר)
סלעים, larger silver coins (one סלע = four זוזים)

phrases.english: "Silver zuzim that are…," and the rest was erased –
phrases.notes: 'That are' is where the number would normally come next, like 'that are fifty.' That number is the part that got erased.

phrases.english: it is no less than two.
"Silver sela'im that are…," and the rest was erased –
it is no less than two.
"Darkonot that are…," and the rest was erased –
it is no less than two.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּסַף זוּזִין דְּאִינּוּן וְנִמְחַק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's rules that limit the lender to the smaller or minimum amount when a שטר is unclear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plural coin word with the number erased means the minimum plural, two coins.

steps.title: When the top and bottom amounts differ, follow the bottom
steps.stepSummary: If one amount is written at the top of the שטר and a different amount at the bottom, we always go by the bottom amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the top of the שטר says a מנה and the bottom says מאתים, or the top says מאתים and the bottom says a מנה, everything follows the bottom.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule: a שטר states the amount in two places, and the two places don't agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is different from step 15. There, we took the smaller amount. Here, we follow the bottom amount even when it is the bigger one. The next steps explain why the top amount is written at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Above, in the top part of the שטר
The lower one, the bottom amount

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with step 15. There, two coin types disagreed, so we took the smaller amount. Here, the top and bottom disagree, and the bottom always wins, even if it is the bigger number.

phrases.english: If it is written in it above, a maneh,
and below, two hundred;
or above, two hundred, and below, a maneh –
everything follows the bottom one.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּתוּב בּוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מָנֶה וּמִלְּמַטָּה מָאתַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case in the same משנה about amounts in a שטר that don't match.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the top and bottom amounts conflict, the bottom amount decides.

steps.title: Then why write the top amount at all?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks: if only the bottom amount counts, what is the point of the top amount?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do they write the top amount?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a question about its own rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the bottom always wins, the top amount seems useless. The משנה wants to explain what job the top amount really does.

keyTerms.meaning: The upper one, the top amount

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן, לָמָה כּוֹתְבִין אֶת הָעֶלְיוֹן?
phrases.english: If so, why do they write the top one?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן לָמָה כּוֹתְבִין אֶת הָעֶלְיוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what purpose the top amount serves, given the rule in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the top amount is for, if the bottom amount always decides.

steps.title: The top amount is a backup
steps.stepSummary: The top amount is there in case a letter in the bottom amount gets erased. Then we can figure out the bottom amount from the top.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that if one letter gets erased from the bottom amount, we can learn it from the top amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers its own question: the top amount is a backup copy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The top amount is not used when it argues with the bottom. Its job is to help when the bottom is damaged and hard to read.

keyTerms.meaning: One can learn it, figure it out

steps.whatToRemember: In a שטר, the bottom amount decides. The top amount is only a backup for when the bottom can't be read.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם תִּמָּחֵק אוֹת אַחַת מִן הַתַּחְתּוֹן –
phrases.english: So that if one letter is erased from the bottom one –
one can learn it from the top one.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁאִם תִּמָּחֵק אוֹת אַחַת מִן הַתַּחְתּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The top amount is a backup for reading the bottom amount if a letter of it gets erased.

steps.title: A ברייתא on vague coin words in a שטר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: plain 'כסף' means at least one silver דינר. 'Silver דינרים' means at least two silver דינרים. 'Silver in דינרים' means silver worth at least two gold דינרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: If he wrote 'כסף', it is no less than one silver דינר. 'Silver דינרים' or 'דינרים silver' means no less than two silver דינרים. 'Silver in דינרים' means no less than silver worth two gold דינרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and brings a ברייתא that explains what vague money words in a שטר mean. The next steps will question its first line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each wording is given its smallest possible meaning. A singular word means one coin, and a plural word means two. The last case is different: 'in דינרים' is read as silver worth two gold דינרים, which is much more money.

keyTerms.meaning: A דינר, a basic silver coin

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Sages taught:
If he said "silver" –
it is no less than a silver dinar.
"Silver dinars" or "dinars silver" –
it is no less than two silver dinars.
"Silver in dinars" –

phrases.aramaic: אֵין פָּחוֹת מִבִּשְׁנֵי דִינָרִין דְּהַב, כֶּסֶף.
phrases.english: it is no less than silver worth two gold dinars.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן אָמַר כֶּסֶף אֵין פָּחוֹת מִדִּינָר כֶּסֶף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא with a ברייתא that adds more cases like the משנה's rules for unclear amounts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vague coin wording gets its smallest reasonable meaning: one דינר for 'כסף' and two for a plural.

steps.title: Why not say 'silver' means just a scrap of silver?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first line of the ברייתא and asks: why should plain 'כסף' mean a full דינר? Maybe it means only a small piece of silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'כסף' means no less than one silver דינר. But why not say it means a piece of silver?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first line of the ברייתא and challenges it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is to give vague wording its smallest meaning. A small lump of silver that is not a coin is worth even less than a דינר. So the גמרא asks why the ברייתא doesn't go even lower.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said (quoting the ברייתא to discuss it)
A piece of silver that is not a coin

phrases.english: The Master said: "Silver" –
it is no less than a silver dinar.
But say it means a piece of silver!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא נְסָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first line of the ברייתא from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that plain 'כסף' means at least one silver דינר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If we always choose the smallest meaning, an uncoined scrap of silver is even smaller than a דינר.

steps.title: The שטר also says 'coin'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers that the ברייתא is talking about a שטר that also wrote the word 'מטבע', so it must mean an actual coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is talking about where the שטר also says 'מטבע' (coin).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the challenge by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the שטר says 'coin', a scrap of silver is ruled out. So the smallest choice is a silver coin.

keyTerms.meaning: Where it is written in it

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
It is where "coin" is written in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְּכָתוּב בֵּיהּ מַטְבֵּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 21.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Plain 'כסף' could mean an uncoined piece of silver.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שטר also says 'מטבע', so it means a silver coin.

steps.title: Why not say it means tiny silver coins?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes further: even if it must be a coin, maybe it means small silver coins (פריטי) worth less than a דינר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why not say it means small coins?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second challenge on the same line of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר's answer proves it is a coin, but it does not prove the coin is a דינר. Smaller silver coins are still coins, and they are worth less.

phrases.english: But say it means small coins!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא פְּרִיטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up challenge after the answer in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that 'כסף' with 'מטבע' means a full דינר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Small silver coins are also coins and are worth less, so the smallest meaning should be one of them.

steps.title: In a place where small silver coins aren't used
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a place where small silver coins are not in use, so the smallest silver coin there is the דינר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is talking about a place where small silver coins do not circulate.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the second challenge, again by narrowing the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where tiny silver coins aren't used, nobody would mean them when writing 'silver coin'. So the smallest real option is a silver דינר, and the ברייתא's ruling stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Plain 'כסף' in a שטר means one silver דינר. This is because the שטר says 'coin' (רבי אלעזר), and because small silver coins aren't used in that place (רב פפא).

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is in a place where silver small coins do not circulate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בְּאַתְרָא דְּלָא סָגֵי פְּרִיטֵי דְכַסְפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to local currency practice
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Silver coin' could mean tiny silver coins.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a place without small silver coins, the smallest silver coin is the דינר.

steps.title: The ברייתא's rules for the word 'gold' in a שטר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: plain 'gold' means at least one gold דינר. 'Gold דינרים' or 'דינרים of gold' means at least two gold דינרים. 'Gold in דינרים' means gold worth at least two silver דינרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If a שטר says 'gold', it means no less than one gold דינר. If it says 'gold דינרים' or 'דינרים of gold', it means no less than two gold דינרים. If it says 'gold in דינרים', it means gold worth no less than two silver דינרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the next part of the ברייתא. It gives the same kind of rules it gave for silver, but now for gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each wording sets a minimum amount, and the lender only collects that minimum. Plain 'gold' means one coin. The plural 'דינרים' means at least two. 'Gold in דינרים' means gold measured by the value of two silver דינרים.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: the opening words of a ברייתא
דינרים, a type of coin; the plural means at least two
'In דינרים': measured by the value of דינרים

steps.confusionAlert: This part is built to match the silver rules from Step 20. Read the two side by side: the same three wordings, but now gold instead of silver.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If it says 'gold', it is no less than a gold דינר.
If it says 'gold דינרים' or 'דינרים of gold',
it is no less than two gold דינרים.
If it says 'gold in דינרים',

phrases.aramaic: – אֵין פָּחוֹת מִבִּשְׁנֵי דִינָרִין כֶּסֶף, דְּהַב.
phrases.english: it is no less than gold worth two silver דינרים.
phrases.notes: The extra בְּ here means 'the value of': you get gold, but only as much as two silver דינרים are worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״דְּהַב״ – אֵין פָּחוֹת מִדִּינָר דְּהַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא from Step 20, moving from silver to gold.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Gold' = at least one gold דינר; 'gold דינרים' or 'דינרים of gold' = at least two gold דינרים; 'gold in דינרים' = gold worth at least two silver דינרים.

steps.title: Why should plain 'gold' mean a whole gold coin?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the first line of the gold section and asks: maybe plain 'gold' means just a small piece of gold, not a full gold דינר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'Gold' means no less than a gold דינר. But why not say it means just a piece of gold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first rule about gold and challenges it. This is the same question it asked about silver in Step 21.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'gold' alone does not say 'coin'. Since the lender only collects the smallest amount the word could mean, a small piece of gold should be enough. So why does the ברייתא give him a whole דינר?

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said: used when the גמרא quotes a line it just brought so it can discuss it
A piece or bar of metal, not a coin

phrases.english: The Master said:
'Gold' is no less than a gold דינר.
But say it means a piece of gold!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: ״דְּהַב״ – אֵין פָּחוֹת מִדִּינָר דְּהַב. אֵימָא נְסָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first rule of the gold section quoted in Step 25, the same way Step 21 challenged the silver rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that plain 'gold' in a שטר means at least one gold דינר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'gold' could mean a lump of gold of any size. Since we follow the smallest possible meaning, a small piece should be enough.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: the שטר also wrote 'coin'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers that the ברייתא is talking about a שטר that also wrote the word 'מטבע', so it must mean a gold coin, and the smallest gold coin is a דינר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: The case is where the שטר also wrote 'coin'.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question with the same answer he gave for silver in Step 22. The שטר wrote the word 'coin', so a lump of gold is ruled out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the שטר says 'coin', a raw piece of gold does not fit the wording. The smallest gold coin is a gold דינר, so that is the minimum the lender collects.
steps.whatToRemember: The gold section works just like the silver section. Plain 'gold' means one gold דינר only because the שטר also wrote 'מטבע' (coin). Without that word, a small piece of gold might be enough.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
It is where 'coin' was written.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: דִּכְתַב ״מַטְבֵּעַ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the ברייתא speaks of a שטר that also wrote 'coin'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Plain 'gold' could mean any small piece of gold.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שטר wrote 'מטבע', so it must mean a gold coin, and the smallest gold coin is a דינר.
